e.t: This word means “to sanctify,” expressing the action of making something holy or setting it apart for God. It describes an act directed toward a person, thing, or name that is treated as holy and dedicated to God’s purpose. The word occurs 28 times in the Greek New Testament, across 25 verses, so it describes a recurring scriptural action rather than a rare or specialized idea. Its common English rendering is “sanctify.”

e.t: This word means “holiness,” referring to the quality of being set apart for God and marked by purity. In the Greek New Testament, it appears three times, and each occurrence is rendered “holiness.” It describes a character or condition that belongs to God’s people and should become evident in their lives. The word points beyond outward religious identity to a life distinguished by devotion to God. Its exact emphasis in any one passage is clarified by the surrounding verse and context.

“Hallelujah” is a praise exclamation—a word spoken or sung to express worship. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs four times, all in Revelation 19, where it is repeated as part of heavenly praise. The word functions as a direct expression of joyful adoration rather than as a person’s name, place, or ordinary description. Its repeated use gives it the character of a communal cry of praise. The Greek New Testament preserves this brief worshipful expression as “hallelujah.”

e.t: Amminadab is a personal name identifying a person rather than a quality, action, or general idea. In the Greek New Testament, it appears three times, in two verses: twice in Matthew 1:4 and once in Luke 3:33. Since the supplied meaning is the name itself, its significance here is identification—distinguishing Amminadab from the other people named in those passages. The surrounding verse text would be needed to explain the name’s specific role in either passage.

e.t: This word describes something located “across from” or “opposite” another place or thing. It points to a position facing or situated on the other side, rather than describing an action or quality. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in Luke 8:26, so its precise force there depends on the surrounding verse and passage. Its basic meaning is a location in relation to something else: across from it or opposite it.

In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in Acts 19:1. The surrounding verse text is needed to explain precisely how the word functions there, but its basic sense remains focused on what is within or farther inside. It is used in John, Acts, and 1 John, showing that the idea appears in different settings while retaining the basic sense of being pleasing.

e.t: This word means “lightning,” the sudden bright flash seen in the sky. In the New Testament, it is used as a noun to refer to visible brightness that appears swiftly and unmistakably. Its use can describe lightning itself or serve as an image of something revealed openly and dramatically, but its basic meaning remains the flash of light. The word occurs nine times in the Greek New Testament, in Matthew, Luke, Revelation, and elsewhere, showing a consistent reference to this striking natural phenomenon.

e.t: This word means to reign—to rule as king or exercise royal authority. It can describe someone who is presently ruling, has ruled, or will rule. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs 21 times and is used both for human rulers and for the lasting authority associated with God’s kingdom. Its wording emphasizes the act or state of ruling, rather than merely holding a royal title. The surrounding verse determines who reigns and when.

This word describes a person who complains or grumbles—“a murmurer” or “grumbler.” It refers to someone whose speech expresses dissatisfaction rather than grateful acceptance. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in Jude 1:16, and is rendered “murmurers.” Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic meaning is a person known for grumbling complaints.

e.t: This Greek verb means “to accuse” someone or “to have accusations brought upon someone.” It describes the act of charging a person with wrongdoing or bringing a complaint against them. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in Luke 16:1. The word expresses an action directed toward another person rather than a general feeling or description. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic meaning is the bringing or making of an accusation.

e.t: This word means “insincere,” describing someone whose speech or conduct is not wholehearted or genuine. It points to a lack of straightforwardness rather than honest agreement or transparent intent. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in 1 Timothy 3:8, so its precise force there depends on the surrounding verse and passage. Its central idea remains clear: a person should not present one thing outwardly while holding or intending something different inwardly.

As a verb expression, it focuses on the act or result of putting something into writing rather than on the document itself. It occurs three times in the Greek New Testament, in Luke and 2 Corinthians. Its exact force in each passage depends on the surrounding verse and what is being written, but the central idea remains written inscription or entry.

e.t: This Greek New Testament word means “to drive” or “to row.” It describes propelling something forward, especially a boat moved by rowing, and can also refer more generally to driving or forcing movement. The word occurs five times in the Greek New Testament, with its uses spread across the Gospels and letters. Its exact force depends on what is being moved in the sentence, but its central idea remains active movement: causing a person, vessel, or other thing to go forward.

e.t: This word means “to mistreat”: to treat someone badly or unfairly. It describes harmful treatment directed toward another person, rather than ordinary disagreement or simple neglect. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs twice, so its meaning is clear but its use is limited to two occurrences. The surrounding verse determines the particular circumstances, while the central idea remains wrongful treatment of someone.

e.t: This word means “decently” or “properly,” describing conduct carried out in an orderly, fitting, and respectable manner. It focuses on how something is done rather than naming the action itself. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs three times, in Romans 13:13, 1 Corinthians 14:40, and 1 Thessalonians 4:12. Across these uses, the word presents behavior that is appropriate and well-ordered, suitable for public conduct and responsible living.

e.t: This word describes being upset, creating commotion, or starting a riot. It can refer to noisy disturbance and disorder rather than quiet concern or private sadness. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs five times, covering situations involving agitation, public disturbance, or an urgent upheaval. Its exact force depends on the surrounding sentence, but the central idea is a disruptive disturbance that unsettles people or a situation.

This word means “look!” and calls attention to something that follows or is being pointed out. It functions as an attention-getting expression, directing the hearer or reader to notice a person, event, statement, or coming action. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs 200 times, so it is a recurring way of focusing attention rather than a term naming an object or idea. Its precise force in any verse depends on what the surrounding sentence presents for notice.

e.t: This word means “as” or “just as,” introducing a comparison or showing that one thing corresponds to another. It helps connect statements by saying that something happens in a similar way, or that one matter should be understood in relation to another. In the Greek New Testament, it appears 13 times across 13 verses, functioning as a linking word rather than naming a person, object, or action. Its precise force in a particular verse depends on the surrounding sentence, but its central purpose is to draw a clear comparison or correspondence.

e.t: This word means “dwelling place,” referring to a location where someone or something resides. It presents the idea of a settled habitation rather than simply a temporary stopping point. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs twice, once in Ephesians and once in Revelation. Its exact significance in either verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its central meaning remains a place prepared or used as a residence.

e.t: Cenchrea is a place-name, referring to a location mentioned in the Greek New Testament. It is not presented here as a general quality, action, or object, but as the name of a specific place. The name occurs twice in the Greek New Testament: once in Acts 18:18 and once in Romans 16:1. Its basic meaning is therefore the proper name “Cenchrea,” while the surrounding verse and passage explain what happened there or why the place is mentioned.

The surrounding verse determines whether the emphasis is on forming an association, remaining attached, or becoming united. The central idea remains close joining or attachment.

Because the word appears only there and the verse text is not included here, its precise force in that sentence must be understood from the surrounding passage. Its central idea remains the removal or ending of a condition regarded as disgraceful.
